newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire says army and rebels fight over Isiro.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says army and rebels fight over Isiro.

text.p: Zaire's army said on Wednesday that it was fighting to defend the northeastern town of Isiro from rebels but acknowledged the fall of Bafwasende in the same region.
"Isiro has not fallen to the rebels. Heavy fighting is still going on there," a senior defence ministry official told Reuters on Wednesday but he added:

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, speaking in the east of the sprawling Central African nation, said earlier his forces captured Isiro on Tuesday and were advancing towards President Mobutu Sese Seko's jungle palace at Gbadolite hundreds of km (miles) to the west.

In Kisangani, headquarters of a counter-offensive launched by the army on January 20, relief officials said more and more trapped Rwandan Hutu refugees were arriving near the village of Tingi Tingi 200 km (125 miles) to the south east.
The Kinshasa official said Bafwasende, 230 km (140 miles) north east of Kisangani, fell on Sunday. Isiro is further north.

The official said on Tuesday that a cargo plane carrying fresh Ugandan troops to fight alongside the rebels had crashed inside Zaire's border in the Ruwenzori mountain area killing some of those on board.

The official, who said Zairean troops had taken prisoner survivors, presented the crash as evidence of direct Ugandan involvement in the fighting -- a charge Kinshasa has also levelled at Rwanda and Burundi.
His comments coincided with a visit to France of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni. "There are no Ugandan troops in Zaire and they will never be," Museveni told reporters.
The rebels, who launched the war in October accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and planning to expel them, hold towns and territory in the east.

They responded to the Zairean army's counter-offensive by attacking on fronts in the north east, southeast and west and have given Mobutu, who had prostate surgery in Europe in August, until February 21 to begin talks on stepping down.
Brenda Barton, spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme in Kisangani, said refugees were flooding Tingi Tingi from Amisi where rebels seized a refugee camp and air strip last week.
Tingi Tingi has one make-shift camp of 120,000 refugees. The new arrivals had formed a second with 35,000 in it, she said.

The Hutu refugees fled Rwanda fearing reprisals following the 1994 genocide by hardline Hutus of minority Tutsis there. Up to 700,000 refugees returned home in December. Those still in Zaire opted to flee west.
